cards.explanation: The answer is that David asks the LORD first. As soon as the report comes in, he inquires of the LORD: "Should I go and attack these Philistines?" And the LORD tells him, "Go and attack the Philistines and save Keilah."

The word is afraid, friends. David's men say it plainly: "Look, we are afraid here in Judah…" Then they ask, "how much more if we go to Keilah against the armies of the Philistines?" I honestly respect them for saying it out loud.

The answer is True. The verse says, "Once again, David inquired of the LORD…" With his men scared, David doesn't just pick a side. He takes the matter straight back to the LORD. I think that's a good habit when everybody around you is nervous and you'd like a steadier voice than your own.

The LORD promises to hand the Philistines over. He says, "…I will deliver the Philistines into your hand." He says it right alongside "Go at once to Keilah…" That's a promise frightened men can lean on, friends. Marching toward an army is easier when the One sending you has already spoken about how it ends.

David's men carried off the Philistines' livestock. The same Philistines who were looting Keilah's threshing floors end up losing their own animals. The text says David and his men struck them "…with a mighty blow." So the livestock came with the win. It's a fair swap, friends.

The answer is that Keilah has gates and bars. Saul says David "…has trapped himself by entering a town with gates and bars." To Saul, those gates and bars are what make it a trap. He even says God has delivered David into his hand.

The answer is False, because the LORD says the opposite. David asks whether Saul will come down, and the answer is, "He will." Then David asks another question, this time about the citizens of Keilah.

The answer is True. David asks, "Will the citizens of Keilah surrender me and my men into the hand of Saul?" and the LORD says, "They will." It's a hard answer to hear, friends, since David just saved those people. But he asked, he got a clear answer, and he knew what to do next.

The answer is that Saul declines to go forth. He had called up his troops, and then he hears David has escaped. The plan fell apart the moment David walked out of the gates. I think a man who was sure he had David trapped has a rough afternoon after that news. Saul doesn't march to Keilah.

The answer is that God won't hand David over. The verse says it directly: "Day after day Saul searched for him, but God would not deliver David into his hand." Saul keeps searching, and it still doesn't work. I think that's the part to remember, friends, when everything looks like it's closing in. God is the One keeping David out of Saul's hands.

The visitor is Jonathan, Saul's son. He "…came to David in Horesh and strengthened his hand in God…" Saul has come out to take David's life, and his own son shows up to encourage him. I think David was glad to see him.

Jonathan says Saul will never lay a hand on David. His words are, "Do not be afraid, for my father Saul will never lay a hand on you." He says it to a man who's being hunted at that very moment. That's a bold thing to tell somebody, friends, and it comes from Saul's own son.

The word is king. Jonathan says, "…you will be king over Israel…" Saul is still on the throne, and Jonathan is talking about what's coming. That's a big thing to say to a man Saul is hunting. I think it's the kind of encouragement a hunted man can use.

The answer is True. Jonathan says, "…you will be king over Israel, and I will be your second-in-command." Jonathan is Saul's son, and he names himself second to David. I think that's a rare kind of friend.
The answer is True. Jonathan says, "Even my father Saul knows this is true." So Saul knows David will be king over Israel. Jonathan says it right after telling David not to be afraid.

The word is covenant. The two of them "…made a covenant before the LORD." A covenant is a formal agreement, friends, and this one is made before the LORD. After that, David remains in Horesh while Jonathan goes home.

The word is hiding. The Ziphites ask Saul, "Is not David hiding among us in the strongholds at Horesh…" They give his hiding place straight to Saul. They even say where it is: the hill of Hachilah, south of Jeshimon. Hiding is the whole situation David is in.

Saul asks the Ziphites to find all of David's hiding places. He tells them, "Observe and find out all the places where he hides. Then come back to me with certainty…" He's been told David is extremely cunning, so he wants the full picture first. He asks them to scout, and he says, "…I will go with you."

The answer is False. When David hears about Saul's search, he "…went down to the rock and stayed in the Wilderness of Maon." So he stays in the same wilderness, friends. Saul hears about it and pursues him there.

A messenger brings news of a raid. Right when Saul is closing in, the messenger says, "Come quickly, for the Philistines have raided the land!" Saul is on one side of the mountain, David is on the other, and then everything changes. It's the kind of interruption you would never plan for, friends. And Saul breaks off the chase.

The answer is True. The messenger says the Philistines have raided the land, and "…Saul broke off his pursuit of David and went to meet the Philistines." The chase just stops. That's why that place is called Sela-hammahlekoth. And David goes up from there.
